extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent practitioners, applicants, and courts (patent attorneys, agents, and advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards governing what constitutes public use, on-sale activity, constructive abandonment, surrender, and the required contents and formalities of patent applications under U.S. law (historical statutes and case law summarized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use constitutes abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor allows his invention to be used by other persons generally, either with or without compensation, then it will be in public use within the meaning of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use results from a transfer of the thing used from inventor to user without reserving control; it need not involve more than one specimen or more than one person knowing of the use; the article need not be visible to the public if ordinary use veils it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design public use by exhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is in public use whenever any article which embodies it, or any picture of it, is exhibited for the purpose of making its character publicly known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibition of articles or pictures to make the design publicly known is sufficient to constitute public use of a design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception (good faith testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use is never public use within the meaning of the statute, if it is conducted in good faith for the purpose of testing the qualities of the invention, and for no other purpose not naturally incidental to that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the experimentation disclosed necessity for improvement is immaterial; secrecy is immaterial; experimentation may be open and long-term (even known to hundreds) if nature of invention requires long testing; inventor may make and sell as many articles as necessary to test and remedy defects without triggering public-use bar, provided primary purpose is honest testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When experimental use becomes public
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use becomes public use when it extends further, either in time, or in number of instances, than is reasonably required to test the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive duration or scope of testing converts experimental activity into public use; courts will consider whether extent of use exceeded reasonable testing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit does not automatically negate experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor uses his invention for profit and not by way of experiment, that is a public use; but incidental profit is not inconsistent with use being only experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main objective being profit (with improvement only incidental) makes use non-experimental; absence of profit does not necessarily make use experimental — context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee use / employer profit does not avoid public-use rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the inventor is but an employee in the place where he uses his invention, or that the profit goes primarily to his employer, does not oust the operation of the public-use rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use by an inventor in employment or profit flowing to employer still counts as inventor's use for public-use analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single specimen/public use sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A single instance of sale of one specimen of the thing invented is enough to constitute putting the invention on sale; and a single publicly used specimen can constitute public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither multiple specimens nor multiple witnesses of use are required to trigger on-sale or public-use bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer for sale qualifies as 'on sale'
rubrics_metrics.description: A device will be on sale within the meaning of the law, if it is offered for sale, whether any specimen of it is actually sold or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An offer to sell can start the statutory clock; actual payment of purchase price is immaterial to the 'on sale' determination for the two-year bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale for experimental purposes exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature of the invention obliges the inventor to put it into the hands of others for crucial experiment, he may sell specimens to them for that purpose, and such a sale will not be obnoxious to the statute, provided there is unequivocal evidence the sale was made for experimental use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor could have tested on his own premises, a sale (absolute or conditional) will be treated as 'on sale' unless clear evidence it was for experimentation; courts require unequivocal evidence of experimental intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale on approval and success rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an inventor furnishes a specimen for use on approval to be paid for if successful, there is an instance of being 'on sale' if the use is successful and the specimen is paid for; if the use is unsuccessful and abandoned, there is no 'on sale' instance even if partly paid while being constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome of the approval/test determines whether the approval transaction counts as an 'on sale' event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale to test commercial merits is 'on sale'
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale for the purpose of testing the commercial merits of an invention will constitute being 'on sale'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transactions aimed at commercial evaluation, even if framed as tests, are treated as on-sale activity that can trigger abandonment bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Made-to-order exception for 'on sale'
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specimen is built or made to order, it is not 'on sale' until it is completed, delivered, and accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts for building to order do not trigger the on-sale bar until completion/delivery/acceptance (acceptance subject to approval by buyer also affects timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of inchoate patent right not a sale
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of the inchoate right to an invention is not such a sale as will be obnoxious to the statute; instead it indicates expectation of obtaining a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer of inchoate rights (e.g., assignment of future patent) is not treated as placing the invention 'on sale' for abandonment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity suffices for constructive abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise identity between the thing covered by the patent and the thing allowed to be in public use or on sale more than two years before application is not necessary; it is enough if the two devices are substantially the same or if the advance did not amount to invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to substantial sameness or whether intervening changes were patentable; mere similarity in function without substantial identity is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making specimen alone not abandonment (except process usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: No constructive abandonment results from mere making of a specimen of an invented thing more than two years before the application; but if invention consists in a process, making a specimen by that process is a use of the process and is governed by the use rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing prototypes alone typically do not trigger the bar unless it constitutes practicing the claimed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale abroad (foreign use) generally not fatal to U.S. patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A public use or sale of a newly invented thing in a foreign country more than two years before the U.S. application will not have the same effect upon a U.S. patent as if it had occurred in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statutory language was ambiguous and some lower courts held otherwise, the Supreme Court held that foreign public use/sale before the U.S. filing does not automatically bar a U.S. patent under the cited Revised Statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use by strangers before two-year period
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use by a stranger, without the knowledge of the inventor, more than two years before the inventor applies for a patent, generally has the same operation of constructive abandonment as public use by the inventor himself; but fraudulent, surreptitious, and piratical uses arising out of a breach of trust do not operate to show abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the inventor continued legitimate experiments until within two years of filing, later independent uses by others might not defeat the patent; fraudulent third-party uses are treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard for experimental use earlier than two years
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of the experimental character of any use which occurred earlier than two years before the application must be full, unequivocal, and convincing, or it cannot prevail to save that patent from invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High burden of proof on inventor to show pre-critical-period activity was experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory two-year bar is inflexible
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory law relevant to constructive abandonment resulting from a public use or from a sale, more than two years before an application for a patent, operates inflexibly upon all cases coming within it and its effect cannot be obviated by any evidence showing reasons for the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will apply the statutory bar strictly regardless of meritorious reasons for delay; exceptions must be statutory or supported by case law (e.g., experimental-use exceptions narrowly construed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment by failure to pay final fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an applicant omits to pay the final fee within six months from allowance and omits to make any new application for the same invention within two years after such allowance, he loses all right to obtain a patent for that invention; the two-year period begins from the date of allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness on post-allowance formalities is critical; only one renewal application may be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive abandonment triggered by certain foreign filings (statutory classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Acts of 1897 and 1903 created classes where failing to file in the U.S. within specified periods after related foreign patents/publications or after foreign filings that resulted in foreign patents can constitute constructive abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for patents applied after 1897, delay of more than two years after a person not in privity obtained a foreign patent or after printed publication may cause abandonment; for some transitional filings (post-1897 to Mar 3, 1903) a seven-month rule applied; for processes/machines/manufactures/compositions after Mar 3, 1903 a 12-month rule applied (day of filing excluded); for designs after Mar 3, 1903 a four-month rule applied. These are statutory timing rules with particular applicability depending on filing date and category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender of patent by formal surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender of an invention may be effected after the grant of letters patent by means of a formal surrender of those letters patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal procedures exist to surrender patents; historical practice acknowledged such mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-use after grant does not automatically cause abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: No abandonment of an invention after the issue of letters patent has been judicially decided to exist in the United States; Congress did not intend constructive abandonment to result from non-use by citizens, and public use after grant does not create a presumption against the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and statutes favor the patentee on non-use; estoppel/acquiescence doctrines are exceptional and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence may support estoppel but needs strong proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence by a patentee in unlicensed use during the life of the patent has sometimes been said to amount to abandonment; however, judges have required strong, continuing acquiescence (without objection and for a series of years) or conduct reasonably inducing belief owner intended to relinquish rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law is inconsistent; to establish abandonment by acquiescence requires clear and convincing factual showing that the patentee intended to relinquish rights (estoppel standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment and related questions are factual and construed for patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions relevant to actual or constructive abandonment are questions of fact; every reasonable doubt should be solved in favor of the patent, for the law does not favor forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial fact-finding and presumptions tilt toward preserving patent rights absent clear proof of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: An application consists of specific formal transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a patent consists of deposit in the Patent Office of a written petition to the Commissioner, deposit of a written specification, making of an oath, payment of the Patent Office fee, and in some cases deposit of drawings, models, or specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications/proceedings are governed by Revised Statutes and Patent Office rules; rules are authoritative unless inconsistent with law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content and who may sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition is signed by the applicant and states name, nationality, residence, present post office address, and requests grant of a patent; petition must be of the inventor, not an assignee (though it may request grant to an assignee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor is insane or dead, guardian/representative/executor/administrator may file; foreign executors need diplomatic/consular proof of authority; statutory provisions specify who may sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification required six parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification properly consists of six parts: (1) the preamble, (2) a general statement of the nature and object of the invention, (3) a brief description of the drawings, if any, (4) a detailed description of the invention, (5) the claim or claims, and (6) the signature of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior witness requirements were removed (1915 amendment); each part has particular functions and must be present to form a proper specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble states the name, present nationality, residence, and present post office address of the applicant and, where acting for an insane or deceased inventor, states the inventor's name, nationality, residence at time of invention and the capacity in which applicant is acting; it also states the title of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble connects petition and specification and identifies parties; accuracy and capacity statements are required where representative acts are taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: General statement must avoid limiting particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Every general statement of the nature and object of the invention should be free from any particularity or limitation which, if imported by implication into one or more of the claims, might reduce the area covered by the patent to territory more narrow than the state of the prior art required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the general statement broadly to avoid inadvertently narrowing claim scope by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of drawings should not repeat details
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of the drawings states what each figure is, but does not state the details of the figures; those details are reserved for the detailed description of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep drawing descriptions high-level, referencing figures; avoid presenting operative details in the figure-listing section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description / enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description must be full enough, and clear enough, and concise enough, and exact enough, to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains (or nearest connected) to make and use the invention (or to compound if a composition, to perform if a process, or to identify if a design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet enablement/specification sufficiency renders any granted patent void; for designs, incorporation by reference to drawing/photograph may suffice.
